text.p: Most metal prices, including gold closed weaker overnight. Oil closed slightly firmer while wheat was little changed. The CRB Index fell 2.32 points to 248.64.

Most base metal markets ended Monday LME trading easier, led by copper, with partial rallies not enough to restore prices to equilibrium, traders said. There was some mid-afternoon stability at the lows throughout the complex, but the buying was largely covering in against early sales, and there was little fresh buying interest. "Copper took a bit of a pasting today, and that really set the tone for the day," one trader said.

Copper prices retreated from early little-changed levels after a modest stock fall of 200 tonnes, with speculative selling and technical pressure driving prices down to $2,475 at one stage. The late covering cut losses slightly, but final business at $2,485 a tonne was still $44 down from last Friday.

Analysts said the approach of the seasonally slow quarter for demand and dwindling supply-side concerns perhaps signalled sentiment may be on the turn. There was little heat in the spreads as well with cash/threes at a slightly softer backwardation of $58. In the short-term, prices may hold this level until a tricky June option declaration on Wednesday is over, some said.

Aluminium flip-flopped either side of $1,600 during the afternoon, with the market damaged by the early decline when chart levels at $1,610 were taken out. Despite a stock fall of 3,825 tonnes, there is some concerns that inventories are building "off-warrant" and that consumer interest is not particularly strong. Prices closed at $1,596, down $23.

Nickel prices bounced back above $7,000 during aftenoon trading, but remained easier after a substantial sell-off earlier in the session. Losses then were induced by the tentative three-year labour agreement at Inco's Sudbury facilities over the weekend and the 1,350-tonne stock increase.

Despite the rally away from the lows, traders expect the market to come under pressure in the short-term, with stocks seen rising further as Russian metal is placed in warrant in Europe. Last business was at $7,025, down $175, but above the $6,910 five-month low hit earlier.

Zinc prices picked up reasonable trade support in the mid-$1,320s, but a partial rally still left the market in the minus column. Short-term technicals are moderately bearish, while softer copper prices were also an influence. Prices closed at $1,330, down $15.
Lead trading was unimpressive, with prices tailing lower from the outset. A modest rally in the afternoon merely reflected trends elsewhere, and final trade was at $626, still down $7.
The tin market staged a fairly robust rally from 14-1/2 month lows of $5,510 racked up this morning, and last business was at $5,640, up $75 from last Friday.

Traders said the market had become oversold in its recent sell-off, so bargain-hunting buying was enough to claw back some lost ground. But the bias remains lower, with $5,500 seen being tested on general technical weakness.

COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended mostly lower, with the exception of silver on Monday, but volumes were low. Uncertainty about the prospects for European Monetary Union (EMU), engendered by the Socialists win in the French elections on Sunday and the dispute between the Bundesbank and German government last week, may provide support for gold longer term, analyst said. But meantime a higher U.S. dollar on Monday, kept pressure on gold, while platinum group metals were hit again by nervousness over the resumption of Russian exports.

"A delay in EMU could lessen the potential of near term supply pressure from European central banks," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said. COMEX August gold ended down $1.00 at $346.50 an ounce, retreating from a ten-day high at $350.40 seen Friday on fund short covering.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $343.30/70 an ounce, compared to the London Monday afternoon fix at $343.90 and the New York close Friday around $344.40/90.

NYMEX crude oil futures prices ended slightly higher Monday, with refined products also posting mild gains, after a non-eventful, lightly traded session. Crude oil for July delivery on rose 10 cents to settle at $20.98 a barrel after trading in a range between $21.17 and $20.83. Traders said the markets were lifeless from start to finish during Monday's session, trading meekly on technical factors because they lack supply-and-demand fundamentals.

CBOT wheat futures closed little changed with concern about the impact of heavy rains on this year's soft red winter crop offset by favorable weather in winter white and hard red winter areas, dealers said. July wheat closed 1/4 cent higher at $3.60-3/4 a bushel. Other months were up 1/4 cent to down three cents.
CSCE world sugar futures settled at their highest level in five-weeks amid fresh, technically-based fund buying. The July contract closed 0.17 cent firmer at 11.34 cents per lb.
